RUN-004.notes: Bounded-concurrency orchestration over the canonical WorkGraph. crates/server/src/runtime/orchestration owns the execution decisions: a deterministic ready queue (priority then id), dependency release (draft/blocked -> ready once every depends_on prerequisite is done; -> blocked when one failed or was cancelled), fan-in joins (a waiting parent joins once its last child is done and is blocked if a child can never finish), a capacity gate counted from durable run state, cancellation propagation down work_nodes.parent_id with dependents blocked, and durable waits obeyed by never selecting a node whose run is parked or suspended. depends_on reads `from` depends on `to` (documented on WorkEdgeKind), so `to` is the prerequisite; orchestration refuses a cyclic snapshot instead of selecting from a graph it cannot reason about. Every started run goes through the existing scheduler RunDispatch port into the canonical Run state machine, so there is no second scheduler or orchestration authority; every node transition goes through a WorkGraphPort whose production implementation applies it as one event-emitting GraphTransaction, proven in crates/graph/tests/orchestration.rs against the real store (one revision bump per batch, a stale replay conflicts, and a dependent is never releasable while any prerequisite is unfinished). Concurrency is counted from durable run state (RUNNING/VERIFYING hold a slot; QUEUED and parked runs do not), so the bound survives a restart and two instances agree; the limit itself is supplied by the caller because RUN-010 owns budget enforcement, and a saturated limit is a typed BUDGET_EXHAUSTED refusal rather than a silent drop. Cancellation converges under a storm: runs go through the one authoritative RuntimeStore::cancel (idempotent, one run.cancelled per run, a lost transaction race counted as already-cancelled), the node batch is revision compare-and-set with bounded recomputation, and work a caller actually cancelled is reported even when a later retry wins the graph race. Two limits are recorded rather than papered over: the Run state machine has no QUEUED -> CANCELLED edge, so an unstarted run inside a cancelled subtree is reported (runs_left_unstarted) and never dispatched instead of being cancelled; and the graph-backed port's wiring belongs to the composition root (APP-001), exactly as PlanWorkspacePort does.

RUN-005.notes: Capability algebra composes grants by intersection with most-restrictive constraints (max_tier=min, approval only toward ask/never, earliest expiry, smallest budget) over all nine DOMAIN §6.1 selector kinds; projection assembly follows the fixed §6.2 layer order, ignores and records any widening as capability.widening_rejected naming the layer, and fails closed with an empty projection plus CAPABILITY_INPUTS_UNAVAILABLE when an input layer is unavailable or a policy has a gap at tier >= 1; authorize() always re-checks the current inputs digest and expiry so a stale projection cannot authorize dispatch; delegation narrowing is implemented for RUN-002's hook. During integration the architecture gate's new-persistent-store rule was corrected: capability owns capability_projections, so it is an allowed store owner, and the rule's fixtures now cover every table-owning module.

RUN-006.notes: Evaluation order is RBAC -> capability projection -> trust escalation -> privacy -> sequence guards -> policy rules -> receipt requirement -> user rules, with tenant and workspace policies merged most-restrictively (deny>ask>allow) and no matching rule at effective tier >= 1 denying. Tier 4 always asks: an always user rule is rejected on store and ignored on evaluation. Receipts bind id/request/effect/approver/params_digest/scope/generation/expiry and are signed with HMAC-SHA256 under a server key from QUANSIO_APPROVAL_SIGNING_KEY (absent key fails closed); verification is constant-time and single-use, so a receipt for one action cannot authorize a changed one, and nothing is written on failure. A parameter change supersedes a pending request with one approval.superseded event. Escalation follows DOMAIN §12 rule 2 (tier >= 2 derived from UNTRUSTED_EXTERNAL escalates one tier) rather than the brief's paraphrase, and escalated proposals cannot use always. Trust labelling arrives through an injected source, fail-closed until INT-012.

RUN-007.notes: Universal Effect Ledger: reservation derives the idempotency key from effect class, resource and params digest and leans on the schema's partial unique in-flight index, so racing dispatchers reserve exactly one action and an in-flight duplicate is a typed conflict; every transition is one event-emitting transaction with exactly one effect.* event and contiguous aggregate versions; settlement is terminal and re-settlement refuses before writing; an OUTCOME_UNKNOWN record cannot be retried (typed refusal) and is resolved only by reconciliation matching the class strategy from config/effects.yaml (validated against the generated catalog and failing closed on any divergence); a retry creates a new identity sharing the key and never touches the old row; approval-required actions cannot bypass the receipt; protocol state keeps next_safe_action on ReconcileEffect until settled; all reads are tenant-scoped.

RUN-008.notes: CompletionContract verification on both sides of the seam. Rust (crates/server/src/runtime/verification) implements DOMAIN.md §4.4: contract.rs parses a WorkNode's contract fail-closed (unknown check kind refused, malformed bound refused, a contract that binds nothing recognised as certifying nothing); checks.rs implements artifact_exists over real artifact metadata (role + min_versions) and effects_settled over the run's EffectRecords, and fails closed naming the owner for test_command (EXEC-006), assertion (no predicate registry yet) and citations_valid (CAP-002), so an unimplemented check can never become a silent pass; service.rs is the ContractVerifier swapped into the engine's existing VerificationPort, so a model claim reaches SUCCEEDED only after every deterministic check passes, human_signoff_required stays a human's decision, and a required semantic verification that is unavailable or disagrees rejects the claim with the verifier's critique as feedback. Python (python/intelligence/evaluation/semantic_verifier) implements the independent verifier itself: GatewaySemanticVerifier builds the verifier call (claim and evidence quoted as data with explicit no-follow instructions), fulfils it through ModelGateway (INT-002) and reads a strict verdict — a response that is not exactly {agrees: bool, critique: non-empty string} is refused, never read as agreement, and a gateway failure is a refusal. Independence is a proof obligation: when the contract requires an independent model and the claimant's model is unnamed, or names this verifier's own model, the verifier refuses. Evidence: six Rust tests drive the real turn loop, verifier and database (false-done, missing artifact then satisfied, unimplemented check fails closed naming EXEC-006, semantic disagreement versus agreement, empty contract, unsettled effect until settled); fifteen Python tests cover the strict verdict contract and independence, drive the shipped verifier with only the transport replaced, and drive the real gateway over loopback against the conformance stub provider (the call is recorded and a non-verdict answer is refused). Recorded limits, not papered over: the cross-process binding between the Rust port and this Python verifier is the RPC boundary's and the composition root's job (INT-001/APP-001), and because a run does not yet record its model route (INT-002/INT-003), the Rust verifier passes claimant_model=None, so a contract requiring independent_model is refused rather than self-certified until that route is recorded.

RUN-009.notes: Recovery, generation fencing and effect reconciliation. crates/server/src/runtime/recovery rebuilds a run's position from durable state only: plan.rs holds the pure decisions (the safe action for a durable position, and the generation fence) and service.rs applies them over the canonical stores. The precedence is the runtime's: honour a cancellation requested before the crash, reconcile an uncertain effect before any further work, stay parked on a wait the run itself owns, and only then resume. Fencing mirrors the runtime's own rule (`Generation::accept`): an actor behind the run's generation is stale and its output is discarded, while a newer generation supersedes the run's — refusing a newer generation would refuse recovery itself, which is why the earlier stricter rule was corrected. Reconciliation is applied from evidence (`ReconciliationEvidence::Determined` when the class has a deterministic check, `Manual` otherwise) and never by dispatching again; a `run.stale_worker_fenced` event records discarded work. `RECOVERY_READ_TABLES` declares the complete read set (runs, turns, steps, attempts, protocol_states via the store, runtime_events, checkpoints, effect_records, evidence, work_nodes) and a structural test scans the module's SQL literals and fails if any other table is referenced — memory tables above all — so 'recovery is not memory' is enforced, not merely intended. Tests: five integration tests drive the shipped Recoverer over real runs, ProtocolState, attempts and EffectRecords — the kill/restart matrix (a run with no pending work resumes, a parked run stays on its own key, a pre-crash cancellation is honoured exactly once and the restart reaches the same logical point), the stale-worker test (recovery refuses a behind generation, the engine refuses its mutation and the run is untouched), the uncertain-effect test (reconciliation is required and named, evidence settles it, exactly one effect row exists and only then does the run resume), and the durable-only and memory-table gates — plus four unit tests over the pure decisions.

RUN-010.notes: Runtime budgets, quotas and capacity control. crates/server/src/runtime/budgets implements DOMAIN.md §13.2: limits.rs holds the pure rules (the seven meters, remaining/fits, the deterministic first-exhausted report, the child<=parent-remaining check and the narrowing helper), and service.rs is the durable authority that grants budgets, charges them and emits usage.* events. Acceptance 2 is enforced at grant time against the parent's REMAINING allowance, not its original limit, and nesting holds through the chain (a grandchild is bounded by its child parent). Acceptance 1 is met twice over: a charge beyond a limit is refused, marks the budget exhausted and emits usage.exhausted, and capacity_limit reports 0 so RUN-004's orchestration gate admits nothing; and the service writes only the budget row and its usage event, so an effect already reserved or dispatched is left untouched for the Effect Ledger — the graceful-stop test asserts an in-flight effect keeps its exact row and that no settlement event appears. RUN-011.notes: The turn loop now owns a real ToolCall path. crates/tools holds the Tool contract and a control-plane Tool Registry loaded from config/tools.yaml: namespaced versioned declarations, a strict JSON-Schema subset whose unknown keywords fail the load (so a schema can never be silently under-enforced), every object schema closing additionalProperties, argument validation that rejects unknown or missing fields, derivation of effect class (static or arg-driven, e.g. fs.write scope), resource selector, canonical parameter digest and idempotency key, per-tool host, output bound, timeout, cancellability, evidence capture and source trust, plus exposure filtered by the capability projection. The generated catalog (schemas/catalog/tools.yaml) and the registry must cover each other exactly; connector/scm families are reserved catalog entries that are not callable until CAP-003 and EXEC-009/012 register concrete operations. crates/server/src/runtime/turn_loop implements DOMAIN §7.4 in the fixed order registry -> schema -> capability projection -> policy/RBAC/user rules -> approval park -> Effect Ledger reservation with a dispatch token -> host execution -> settlement, with the durable tool_calls row (migration 0007 records the declaration version) and tool.* RuntimeEvents. Independent calls are dispatched concurrently and their results applied in proposal order; the engine now parks a run for approval, resumes the recorded call instead of re-proposing it, and reports an unsettled effect for reconciliation rather than re-dispatching. The question protocol (user.ask and the model's question) writes a durable Question with the policy TTL, parks WAITING_QUESTION and resumes on the answer or expires the run; delegation, plan and memory routes go to their owning ports and fail closed with the owner named. Fail-closed choices: a refusal before the reservation writes no EffectRecord and reaches no host; the proposal's causal chain is evaluated from UNTRUSTED_EXTERNAL until INT-005 supplies real context labels, so a tier >= 2 call is escalated and needs a receipt. INT-009.notes: Skill registry, promotion ladder and task-scoped resolver, both halves, unblocked by the container runtime coming back. The control plane (crates/server/src/control/skills) owns the rows: `state.rs` is the §11.5 ladder as a fail-closed state machine (DRAFT → CANDIDATE → EVALUATING → APPROVED → ACTIVE → DEPRECATED → RETIRED, with EVALUATING → REJECTED; only ACTIVE resolves), and `store.rs` is the durable registry — create a skill, add a DRAFT version, promote along the ladder. Every mutation is one transaction that stages its `skill.*` RuntimeEvent (`skill.created`, `skill.version_created`, `skill.version_promoted`) at the aggregate's next version, so a refused promotion writes neither the state nor the event; the refusal travels out of band as `MutationRejected` and comes back typed (VALIDATION_SCHEMA / RUNTIME_ILLEGAL_TRANSITION / NOT_FOUND / CONFLICT_STATE / INTERNAL). One invariant is the store's rather than the ladder's: a skill has at most one ACTIVE version and `skills.current_active_version_id` names exactly that version — promoting to ACTIVE is refused while a different version is active (deprecate it first, which is the ladder's own ACTIVE → DEPRECATED edge), leaving ACTIVE clears the pointer, and `active_versions` (the view the resolver consumes) requires the state and the pointer to agree, ordered by name so the resolver's input order is deterministic. The Python resolver (python/intelligence/skills) resolves at most `max_skills` ACTIVE versions relevant to the task, excluding any candidate whose tool_needs or capability_needs exceed the caller's snapshot rather than granting them, and accounting for every candidate it excludes with the rule that excluded it. The rules: chunking.py chunks a source deterministically on paragraph, then sentence, then word boundaries and keys every chunk by the sha256 of its text, so an edit re-embeds its tail rather than the document; provider.py embeds through an ordered route list that refuses a candidate whose width differs from the index before any call (failover moves between endpoints, never between embedding spaces) and records every attempt; index.py is the index itself, keyed by tenant, workspace, source kind, source ref, model, snapshot, content digest and chunk index, with incremental re-embedding, deletion propagation, a pruning full rebuild and a semantic query returning provenance. Cross-tenant retrieval is impossible by construction: an EmbeddingIndex is bound to one tenant, no public method accepts one, every statement carries the filter and the table's forced RLS gets a context on every operation. THE WIRE (this run): model_gateway/embeddings.py answers the `embedding` request class with a non-streaming fulfilment through the one gateway - the same deterministic route resolution, credential custody, DLP guard and pinned transport as a chat call, with only the response shape differing - and refuses a payload that does not cover every input exactly once or whose width is not the route's declared width. ModelGateway.embed resolves the embedding class through INT-003's PolicyRouteSelector (the conversation selector is class-blind and would send an embedding call to a chat model); embedding_routes() reports the failover candidates, filtered to models that declare both the `embeddings` capability and a width. gateway_provider.py joins that to the index: one GatewayEmbeddingProvider per catalog route, composed by gateway_embedder into a FailoverEmbedder pinned to INDEX_DIMENSIONS, so a route of another width is refused at composition. The servicer's `Embed` validates the scope, the request shape and any named route, then returns one vector per input at the width actually served. AUTHORITATIVE SOURCES (this run): sources.py reads the authoritative source plane through two ports - a listing the source's owner supplies, and read-only object bytes - with ArtifactObjectListing implementing the CORE-007 object-key layout (tenants/<tenant>/artifacts/<artifact>/versions/<version>/<sha256>) and objectstore.py implementing the object bytes with a stdlib SigV4 GET (list + get only: writing artifact bytes is the Rust authority's job, so the intelligence plane ships no write surface).
